Details

Conflicting evidence14Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17 min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state. A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a…
  • Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17not traced min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state.
  • A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a median incision-to-closure time of 38 min, same-day discharge, low pain and no recurrences. Suggests operative time and recovery can match or beat laparoscopy at the steady state.
  • Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months.
  • A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data.
  • Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion.
  • A 2026 narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion.
  • Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98% (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17not traced min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. Say 'variable, often longer', not 'longer'.
  • Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139not traced) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14 d (39% vs 5%), but it is small (n=59), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
  • Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258 vs $1421, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade. The 2026 RCT MA reported no significant cost difference on low or very-low certainty evidence (42625069), so state that the cost direction is consistent but the certainty is low.
  • Long-term outcomes (chronic pain, recurrence, quality of life) are essentially unproven. The only RCT long-term data are RIVAL at 1-2 years with about 25% loss to follow-up (35578051). Absence of evidence of benefit does not equal evidence of no benefit. Recurrence differences in observational meta-analyses (42541618not traced, RR 0.32) are low certainty and confounded.
  • Complex, recurrent, bilateral, obese and inguinoscrotal hernias: no RCT has addressed these subgroups. The conclusion applies to mostly primary, unilateral hernias in selected, experienced-surgeon settings. Robotic advantages there are plausible but untested (prospective SCAR study is only a protocol, 42040509not traced).
  • Evidence base is low or very-low certainty and heterogeneous: small trials, mostly rTAPP vs lTAPP (only ROGER used lTEP as comparator), mostly high-income expert centres, an Indian RCT (42527734) null, and an open-console platform in VOLTAIRE. Findings may not generalise to other platforms (Hugo, Dexter, Versius) or to trainee surgeons.
  • Surgeon-side benefits are the most consistent robotic signal (ergonomics in VOLTAIRE and a 2026 ergonomics MA 42842114not traced, lower NASA-TLX workload in ROGER) but they are not patient outcomes. Surgeon-side benefits should be reported separately from the patient-outcome verdict.
  • No HerniaSurge or EHS guideline statement on robotic versus laparoscopic inguinal repair was found in PubMed. Do not claim a guideline position. The only society item is an EHS training pathway (40842882), which is not a recommendation to prefer either approach.

Verdict: the conclusion holds with caveats.

Caveats
  • Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98%not verified (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17not verified min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. Say 'variable, often longer', not 'longer'.
  • Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139not verified) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14not verified d (39%not verified vs 5%not verified), but it is small (n=59not verified), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
  • Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258not verified vs $1421not verified, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade. The 2026not verified RCT MA reported no significant cost difference on low or very-low certainty evidence (42625069), so state that the cost direction is consistent but the certainty is low.
  • Long-term outcomes (chronic pain, recurrence, quality of life) are essentially unproven. The only RCT long-term data are RIVAL at 1not verified-2 years with about 25%not verified loss to follow-up (35578051). Absence of evidence of benefit does not equal evidence of no benefit. Recurrence differences in observational meta-analyses (42541618not verified, RR 0.32not verified) are low certainty and confounded.
  • Complex, recurrent, bilateral, obese and inguinoscrotal hernias: no RCT has addressed these subgroups. The conclusion applies to mostly primary, unilateral hernias in selected, experienced-surgeon settings. Robotic advantages there are plausible but untested (prospective SCAR study is only a protocol, 42040509not verified).
  • Evidence base is low or very-low certainty and heterogeneous: small trials, mostly rTAPP vs lTAPP (only ROGER used lTEP as comparator), mostly high-income expert centres, an Indian RCT (42527734) null, and an open-console platform in VOLTAIRE. Findings may not generalise to other platforms (Hugo, Dexter, Versius) or to trainee surgeons.
  • Surgeon-side benefits are the most consistent robotic signal (ergonomics in VOLTAIRE and a 2026not verified ergonomics MA 42842114not verified, lower NASA-TLX workload in ROGER) but they are not patient outcomes. Surgeon-side benefits should be reported separately from the patient-outcome verdict.
  • No HerniaSurge or EHS guideline statement on robotic versus laparoscopic inguinal repair was found in PubMed. Do not claim a guideline position. The only society item is an EHS training pathway (40842882), which is not a recommendation to prefer either approach.
Evidence against
  • Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17not verified min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state.
    “Among studies using operative-time-based CUSUM analyses, a median threshold of 32 cases was associated with improved operative efficiency in rTAPP, as reflected by reduced operative time.”
    PMID 42747553
  • A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a median incision-to-closure time of 38 min, same-day discharge, low pain and no recurrences. Suggests operative time and recovery can match or beat laparoscopy at the steady state.
    “The overall operative duration from incision to closure was a median of 38 min, while total theatre time (wheels in to wheels out) was a median of 68 min.”
    PMID 42198825
  • Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months.
    “The median operative time was 56 min for unilateral and 101 min for bilateral repair. Four (3.3%) rTAPP patients experienced complications, with two recurrences at the 6-month follow-up.”
    PMID 40842882
  • A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data.
    “While complex inguinal hernia repairs have traditionally been relative contraindication for laparoscopic repair due to technical difficulties, the robotic approach may help overcome these challenges.”
    PMID 42272915
  • Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion.
    “This has been attributed to training challenges, steep learning curve, and limited evidence of benefit for bilateral and recurrent hernias.”
    PMID 41938185
  • A 2026not verified narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion.
    “Robotic-assisted repair may offer ergonomic and educational advantages, but evidence of superior patient outcomes is limited, while operative times and costs are generally higher than with conventional laparoscopy.”
    PMID 42658055

Edit & re-run

At a glance: No consistent patient benefit; costs more.

  • Cost: $3258 robotic vs $1421 laparoscopic [1]

Main caveat: Small trials with short follow-up.

Bottom line

No consistent patient benefit; longer and costlier [1].

Certainty: Low small, heterogeneous trials

What this means for clinical practice

Default choice
Laparoscopic repair.
Who may benefit
Not shown.
Counselling
Recovery is similar.
Cost per case
not known in India; $3258 vs $1421 in RIVAL

Conflicting evidence

  • Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17not traced min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state.
  • A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a median incision-to-closure time of 38 min, same-day discharge, low pain and no recurrences. Suggests operative time and recovery can match or beat laparoscopy at the steady state.
  • Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months.
  • A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data.
  • Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion.
  • A 2026 narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion.
  • Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98% (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17not traced min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. Say 'variable, often longer', not 'longer'.
  • Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139not traced) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14 d (39% vs 5%), but it is small (n=59), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
  • Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258 vs $1421, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade. The 2026 RCT MA reported no significant cost difference on low or very-low certainty evidence (42625069), so state that the cost direction is consistent but the certainty is low.
  • Long-term outcomes (chronic pain, recurrence, quality of life) are essentially unproven. The only RCT long-term data are RIVAL at 1-2 years with about 25% loss to follow-up (35578051). Absence of evidence of benefit does not equal evidence of no benefit. Recurrence differences in observational meta-analyses (42541618not traced, RR 0.32) are low certainty and confounded.
  • Complex, recurrent, bilateral, obese and inguinoscrotal hernias: no RCT has addressed these subgroups. The conclusion applies to mostly primary, unilateral hernias in selected, experienced-surgeon settings. Robotic advantages there are plausible but untested (prospective SCAR study is only a protocol, 42040509not traced).
  • Evidence base is low or very-low certainty and heterogeneous: small trials, mostly rTAPP vs lTAPP (only ROGER used lTEP as comparator), mostly high-income expert centres, an Indian RCT (42527734) null, and an open-console platform in VOLTAIRE. Findings may not generalise to other platforms (Hugo, Dexter, Versius) or to trainee surgeons.
  • Surgeon-side benefits are the most consistent robotic signal (ergonomics in VOLTAIRE and a 2026 ergonomics MA 42842114not traced, lower NASA-TLX workload in ROGER) but they are not patient outcomes. Surgeon-side benefits should be reported separately from the patient-outcome verdict.
  • No HerniaSurge or EHS guideline statement on robotic versus laparoscopic inguinal repair was found in PubMed. Do not claim a guideline position. The only society item is an EHS training pathway (40842882), which is not a recommendation to prefer either approach.

Guidelines and consensus statements

  • European Hernia Society: mesh repair for adults — “Mesh repair is recommended for all adults with an inguinal hernia.” [2]

Challenged by the skeptic

Verdict: the conclusion holds with caveats.

Caveats

  • Operative time is NOT consistently longer with robotic repair. The RCTs conflict: DIRECT (40632168) and ROLAIS (40277023) found robotic faster, while RIVAL, ROGER and VOLTAIRE found it longer. The MA pooled difference is non-significant with I2 about 98%not verified (42927985). The learning curve (about 32 cases, 17not verified min, 42747553) and surgeon experience probably drive this. Say 'variable, often longer', not 'longer'.
  • Not every RCT found 'no benefit'. ROLAIS (40277023, n=139not verified) reported fewer complications, less inflammation and more same-day discharge with robotic repair, but it is open-label and single-centre. VOLTAIRE (40450465) found more patients back to normal activity at 14not verified d (39%not verified vs 5%not verified), but it is small (n=59not verified), a secondary outcome and unblinded. The honest summary is 'no consistent patient benefit across trials, with two trials showing early signals'.
  • Cost is the most robust finding against robotic repair (RIVAL $3258not verified vs $1421not verified, and several observational and model studies). The cost data come mostly from observational or modelled studies plus one RCT. Costs depend on the platform and the institution and are not RCT-grade. The 2026not verified RCT MA reported no significant cost difference on low or very-low certainty evidence (42625069), so state that the cost direction is consistent but the certainty is low.
  • Long-term outcomes (chronic pain, recurrence, quality of life) are essentially unproven. The only RCT long-term data are RIVAL at 1not verified-2 years with about 25%not verified loss to follow-up (35578051). Absence of evidence of benefit does not equal evidence of no benefit. Recurrence differences in observational meta-analyses (42541618not verified, RR 0.32not verified) are low certainty and confounded.
  • Complex, recurrent, bilateral, obese and inguinoscrotal hernias: no RCT has addressed these subgroups. The conclusion applies to mostly primary, unilateral hernias in selected, experienced-surgeon settings. Robotic advantages there are plausible but untested (prospective SCAR study is only a protocol, 42040509not verified).
  • Evidence base is low or very-low certainty and heterogeneous: small trials, mostly rTAPP vs lTAPP (only ROGER used lTEP as comparator), mostly high-income expert centres, an Indian RCT (42527734) null, and an open-console platform in VOLTAIRE. Findings may not generalise to other platforms (Hugo, Dexter, Versius) or to trainee surgeons.
  • Surgeon-side benefits are the most consistent robotic signal (ergonomics in VOLTAIRE and a 2026not verified ergonomics MA 42842114not verified, lower NASA-TLX workload in ROGER) but they are not patient outcomes. Surgeon-side benefits should be reported separately from the patient-outcome verdict.
  • No HerniaSurge or EHS guideline statement on robotic versus laparoscopic inguinal repair was found in PubMed. Do not claim a guideline position. The only society item is an EHS training pathway (40842882), which is not a recommendation to prefer either approach.

Evidence against, and guidelines

  • Learning curve: operative time in rTAPP falls significantly after about 32 cases. Pooled early-versus-late operative time gap is 17not verified min. Trial operative-time penalties may therefore reflect early learning curve, not steady-state. — “Among studies using operative-time-based CUSUM analyses, a median threshold of 32 cases was associated with improved operative efficiency in rTAPP, as reflected by reduced operative time.” PMID 42747553
  • A high-volume robotic surgeon past the learning curve reports a median incision-to-closure time of 38 min, same-day discharge, low pain and no recurrences. Suggests operative time and recovery can match or beat laparoscopy at the steady state. — “The overall operative duration from incision to closure was a median of 38 min, while total theatre time (wheels in to wheels out) was a median of 68 min.” PMID 42198825
  • Uncontrolled UK learning-curve series supports the safety of a structured EHS training pathway. Median rTAPP time was 56 min unilateral and 101 min bilateral. Complications were 3.3% and there were 2 recurrences at 6 months. — “The median operative time was 56 min for unilateral and 101 min for bilateral repair. Four (3.3%) rTAPP patients experienced complications, with two recurrences at the 6-month follow-up.” PMID 40842882
  • A technique report asserts a theoretical robotic advantage in complex hernias. It is opinion and a single case, with no outcome data. — “While complex inguinal hernia repairs have traditionally been relative contraindication for laparoscopic repair due to technical difficulties, the robotic approach may help overcome these challenges.” PMID 42272915
  • Narrative review states the evidence for MIS in bilateral and recurrent hernias is limited. This supports the gap in the evidence base rather than refuting the conclusion. — “This has been attributed to training challenges, steep learning curve, and limited evidence of benefit for bilateral and recurrent hernias.” PMID 41938185
  • A 2026not verified narrative review is consistent with the researcher's conclusion. — “Robotic-assisted repair may offer ergonomic and educational advantages, but evidence of superior patient outcomes is limited, while operative times and costs are generally higher than with conventional laparoscopy.” PMID 42658055
  • A guideline recommends mesh repair — “Mesh repair is recommended for all adults with an inguinal hernia.” [2]
  • European Hernia Society: mesh repair for adults — “Mesh repair is recommended for all adults with an inguinal hernia.” [2]

Other notable findings from this run

  • The extractor could not match 45 numbers to the papers' wording; they are kept and labelled “not verified” in the trials table. [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [9] [10]
  • DIRECT reports surgeon experience inconsistently [1].

Completeness: 1 gap found; 1 added
